context: For Heraclitus the logos is the rational order that runs through all change, which most people fail to notice. Later Greek thinkers used the same word for argument, definition and the reasoning faculty itself. The Stoics made it the divine reason pervading the cosmos, and John's Gospel opens with it.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ψυχῆς πείρατα ἰὼν οὐκ ἂν ἐξεύροιο, πᾶσαν ἐπιπορευόμενος ὁδόν· οὕτω βαθὺν λόγον ἔχει
quote.translation: You would not find the limits of the soul by going, though you travelled every road: so deep a logos does it have.

image.credit: Johannes Moreelse · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The first Greek philosophers asked what the archē of everything is: the source from which things come and into which they return. Thales said water, Anaximenes air, Anaximander 'the boundless'. The same word also means 'rule' or 'command', so a first principle is also what governs.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: Ἀρχὴν δὲ τῶν πάντων ὕδωρ ὑπεστήσατο
quote.translation: He made water the first principle of all things.

image.credit: Sailko · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Anaximander's candidate for the first principle: not any one element but something without limits or definite character. Opposites like hot and cold separate out of it and pay each other 'penalty' for their injustice. It is the first abstract concept in Western philosophy.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: οὗτος ἔφασκεν ἀρχὴν καὶ στοιχεῖον τὸ ἄπειρον
quote.translation: He said that the first principle and element is the boundless.

image.credit: Attributed to Pietro Bellotti · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Physis is the way a thing grows and behaves of its own accord, as opposed to what is made by craft or fixed by custom (nomos). The early thinkers were called physikoi because they studied it. The contrast between physis and nomos drove fifth-century debates about whether justice is natural or conventional.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: φύσις λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ἡ τῶν φυομένων γένεσις
quote.translation: 'Nature' means in one sense the genesis of growing things.

image.credit: Johannes Moreelse · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Nomos covers both written law and unwritten custom. The Sophists set it against physis: some argued that conventional justice restrains the strong against nature, others that law is what makes human life possible. Plato's dialogues return to the question again and again.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ὡς τὰ πολλὰ δὲ ταῦτα ἐναντί' ἀλλήλοις ἐστίν, ἥ τε φύσις καὶ ὁ νόμος
quote.translation: For the most part these two are opposed to each other: nature and convention.

image.credit: Jusepe de Ribera · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Aretē is the excellence of anything at doing what it does: a knife's sharpness, a horse's speed, a person's goodness. Socrates asked whether human aretē could be taught, and Plato and Aristotle identified it with the virtues of character and intellect. 'Virtue' is the usual translation, but 'excellence' is closer.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ΜΕΝ. καὶ ἄλλαι πάμπολλαι ἀρεταί εἰσιν, ὥστε οὐκ ἀπορία εἰπεῖν ἀρετῆς πέρι ὅτι ἐστίν·
quote.translation: MENO: And there are a great many other virtues, so it is no trouble to say what virtue is.

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Aporia is the puzzled state in which an argument leaves you stuck. Socrates' early dialogues often end there: the confident speaker discovers he cannot define courage or piety after all. Aristotle made working through aporiai the standard way to begin an inquiry.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: σὺ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ αὐτός τε ἀπορεῖς καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιεῖς ἀπορεῖν
quote.translation: you do nothing but get into difficulties yourself and make others get into difficulties.

image.credit: Copy of Lysippos (?) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The elenchus is Socrates' method: get someone to state what they believe, then draw out further admissions until they contradict the original claim. It shows the speaker does not know what he thought he knew. Socrates claimed his only wisdom was knowing that he did not know.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ
quote.translation: The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.

image.credit: Copy of Lysippos (?) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Plato's Forms (eidē, also ideai) are the unchanging realities that particular things imitate: many beautiful things, one Beauty itself. Only the Forms can be truly known, while the changing world of the senses gives mere opinion. Aristotle kept the word but placed form inside things, as their structure.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: εἶδος γάρ πού τι ἓν ἕκαστον εἰώθαμεν τίθεσθαι περὶ ἕκαστα τὰ πολλά, οἷς ταὐτὸν ὄνομα ἐπιφέρομεν
quote.translation: We are accustomed to positing one single Form for each set of many things to which we apply the same name.

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: In the Meno and Phaedo, Plato argues that learning is really remembering what the soul knew before birth. Socrates leads an untaught slave boy to a geometric truth only by asking questions. The theory is the ancestor of later doctrines of innate ideas.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: τὸ γὰρ ζητεῖν ἄρα καὶ τὸ μανθάνειν ἀνάμνησις ὅλον ἐστίν
quote.translation: For seeking and learning are, after all, wholly recollection.

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Plato and Aristotle both say philosophy begins in wonder: puzzlement at something we do not understand. Socrates tells young Theaetetus that his dizziness at a paradox is a sign of a philosophical nature.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: μάλα γὰρ φιλοσόφου τοῦτο τὸ πάθος, τὸ θαυμάζειν· οὐ γὰρ ἄλλη ἀρχὴ φιλοσοφίας ἢ αὕτη
quote.translation: For this feeling, wonder, belongs very much to the philosopher: there is no other beginning of philosophy than this.

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: In Plato's Symposium, Diotima teaches Socrates that erōs is longing for what we lack, above all for the beautiful. Rightly guided, it climbs a ladder from one beautiful body to beautiful souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to Beauty itself. Here 'Platonic love' has its origin.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ἔστιν ἄρα συλλήβδην, ἔφη, ὁ ἔρως τοῦ τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὑτῷ εἶναι ἀεί
quote.translation: In sum, she said, love is of having the good for oneself always.

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Aristotle argues that the highest human good is eudaimonia, a whole life lived well, not a passing feeling of happiness. It consists in activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, above all reason. 'Flourishing' captures it better than 'happiness'.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: τὸ ἀνθρώπινον ἀγαθὸν ψυχῆς ἐνέργεια γίνεται κατ' ἀρετήν
quote.translation: The human good turns out to be activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: For Aristotle, to understand a thing you must know its telos, what it is for. An acorn's telos is the oak, an eye's is seeing. Explanation by ends (teleology) dominated natural philosophy until the scientific revolution, and it survives in ethics.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ἡ δὲ φύσις τέλος ἐστίν
quote.translation: And nature is an end.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Epistēmē is knowledge in the strict sense: understanding why something must be so, demonstrated from first principles. Plato contrasted it with doxa, mere opinion. Aristotle made it one of the intellectual virtues, alongside technē and phronēsis. It gives us 'epistemology'.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ἡ μὲν ἄρα ἐπιστήμη ἐστὶν ἕξις ἀποδεικτική
quote.translation: Scientific knowledge, then, is a demonstrative state.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Technē is skilled know-how that produces something: medicine, shipbuilding, rhetoric. Socrates used it as a model of expert knowledge that can give an account of itself. Aristotle separated it from epistēmē (knowing what cannot be otherwise) and phronēsis (acting well).
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ταὐτὸν ἂν εἴη τέχνη καὶ ἕξις μετὰ λόγου ἀληθοῦς ποιητική
quote.translation: craft would be the same as a productive state involving true reasoning.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Phronēsis is the ability to see what to do in particular situations, here and now. For Aristotle no one can be fully virtuous without it, and it cannot be learned from rules alone: it needs experience. It came back into favour in 20th-century virtue ethics.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: λείπεται ἄρα αὐτὴν εἶναι ἕξιν ἀληθῆ μετὰ λόγου πρακτικὴν περὶ τὰ ἀνθρώπῳ ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακά
quote.translation: It remains, then, that it is a true state involving reason, concerned with action about what is good and bad for a human being.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Aristotle coined energeia for actuality, as opposed to dynamis, potentiality. A sleeping geometer has knowledge potentially; when she proves a theorem she has it actually. The pair let him explain change without Parmenides' paradoxes. Our word 'energy' descends from it.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ἔστι δὴ ἐνέργεια τὸ ὑπάρχειν τὸ πρᾶγμα μὴ οὕτως ὥσπερ λέγομεν δυνάμει
quote.translation: Actuality, then, is the thing's existing, not in the way we call potential.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Ousia, from the verb 'to be', is Aristotle's word for what is most fundamentally real. In the Categories it is the individual thing, this horse or this man; in the Metaphysics the inquiry shifts to form. Latin rendered it substantia and essentia, and Christian theology used it for the one nature of the Trinity.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: καὶ δὴ καὶ τὸ πάλαι τε καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ ζητούμενον καὶ ἀεὶ ἀπορούμενον, τί τὸ ὄν, τοῦτό ἐστι τίς ἡ οὐσία
quote.translation: And indeed the question asked long ago, now, and always, and always puzzled over, 'what is being?', is the question 'what is substance?'

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Ataraxia is freedom from mental disturbance, the goal shared by Epicureans and Sceptics. Epicurus sought it by removing the fear of death and of gods; the Sceptics by suspending judgement (epochē), after which tranquillity follows 'like a shadow'.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: τέλος δὲ οἱ σκεπτικοί φασι τὴν ἐποχήν, ᾗ σκιᾶς τρόπον ἐπακολουθεῖ ἡ ἀταραξία
quote.translation: The Sceptics say the goal is suspension of judgement, which tranquillity follows like a shadow.

image.credit: Eric Gaba · CC BY-SA 2.5 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The Stoic sage is free of the pathē, the irrational passions such as fear, grief and lust, which the Stoics thought were mistaken judgements. Apatheia is not indifference: the wise still have 'good feelings' like joy. The English 'apathy' has lost this sense.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: Φασὶ δὲ καὶ ἀπαθῆ εἶναι τὸν σοφόν, διὰ τὸ ἀνέμπτωτον εἶναι
quote.translation: They say the wise man is also free from passion, because he is not prone to fall into it.

image.credit: William Sonmans / Michael Burghers · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The Pyrrhonian Sceptics answered every claim with an equally strong counter-claim and so 'held back' from assent. Husserl revived the word in the 20th century for bracketing the question of whether the world exists, in order to describe experience exactly.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: περὶ τῶν δογματικῶν ζητήσεων ἐπέχειν, οὐ περὶ τῶν βιωτικῶν
quote.translation: to suspend judgement about dogmatic inquiries, not about the business of living.

image.credit: Unknown author · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Stoic ethics starts from oikeiōsis: every animal from birth treats itself as its own and cares for its survival. In humans this concern widens, like circles round the self, to family, city and finally all humanity. It grounds Stoic cosmopolitanism.

quote.text: οἰκειούσης αὑτῷ τῆς φύσεως ἀπ' ἀρχῆς
quote.translation: since nature from the beginning makes it at home with itself.

image.credit: William Sonmans / Michael Burghers · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Aristotle defines the human being as an animal made by nature for life in a polis. Anyone who can live without a city is either a beast or a god. Speech (logos), which lets us share ideas of the just and unjust, is what makes us political.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ὁ ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον
quote.translation: man is by nature a political animal.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The idea that the mind begins with no content of its own goes back to Aristotle, who compared the intellect to a writing tablet with nothing written on it. Medieval Latin called it tabula rasa. Locke made it the emblem of empiricism: all ideas come from experience.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 10615

quote.text: Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas
quote.translation: (Original English: Locke's 'white paper' is his version of the tabula rasa.)

image.credit: Godfrey Kneller · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: A priori knowledge is known independently of experience, as in mathematics or logic; a posteriori knowledge depends on it. Scholastics used the terms for reasoning from causes to effects and back. Kant reshaped them and asked how synthetic a priori judgements are possible.

quote.text: In allen theoretischen Wissenschaften der Vernunft sind synthetische Urteile a priori als Prinzipien enthalten
quote.translation: In all theoretical sciences of reason synthetic judgements a priori are contained as principles.

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Duns Scotus asked what makes an individual this one and not another. His answer was a haecceitas, a positive principle of individuality distinct from the shared nature. The term has been revived in modern metaphysics for primitive identity.

quote.text: Non est igitur 'ista entitas' materia vel forma vel compositum, in quantum quodlibet istorum est 'natura', - sed est ultima realitas entis quod est materia vel quod est forma
quote.translation: So 'this entity' is not matter or form or the composite, insofar as each of these is a 'nature', but it is the ultimate reality of the being that is matter or that is form.

image.credit: Justus van Gent / Pedro Berruguete · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Quidditas is what a thing is: the answer to 'what is it?' (quid est?). Latin scholastics coined it to render Arabic and Greek terms for essence. Aquinas uses it for the essence expressed by a definition, as distinct from a thing's existence (esse).

quote.text: nomen essentiae a philosophis in nomen quiditatis mutatur
quote.translation: the philosophers change the name 'essence' into the name 'quiddity'.

context: Aquinas, following Aristotle, describes God as pure actuality, with no unrealised potential. Since change is passing from potential to actual, God cannot change, lack anything, or be composed of parts. It is the Latin heir of Aristotle's unmoved mover.

quote.text: Deus est purus actus, non habens aliquid de potentialitate
quote.translation: God is pure act, having nothing of potentiality.

context: For Aquinas a creature's essence (what it is) is distinct from its esse (that it is). Only in God are they identical: God is ipsum esse subsistens, subsisting being itself. The distinction, prepared by Avicenna, is central to Thomist metaphysics.

quote.text: Aliquid enim est, sicut Deus, cuius essentia est ipsummet suum esse
quote.translation: For there is something, namely God, whose essence is his very act of being itself.

context: Descartes doubts everything that can be doubted, even mathematics, and finds one thing he cannot: that he is thinking, and so exists. quote.text: je pense, donc je suis
quote.translation: I think, therefore I am.

context: Descartes divides reality into two substances: res cogitans, mind, whose essence is thought, and res extensa, matter, whose essence is extension in space. How the two interact in a human being became the mind–body problem.

context: Spinoza holds that each thing, as far as it can, strives to persevere in its being, and that this striving is its very essence. Desire, joy and sadness are all variations of it. Hobbes and Leibniz used the term too, but Spinoza's version is the best known.

quote.text: Unaquæque res quantum in se est, in suo esse perseverare conatur.
quote.translation: Each thing, as far as it is in itself, strives to persevere in its being.

context: Leibniz's monads are simple, partless substances, the ultimate constituents of reality. They have no windows: nothing enters or leaves them, and each mirrors the whole universe from its own point of view. Their harmony is pre-established by God.

quote.text: Erst das Christenthum, mit seinem Ressentiment gegen das Leben auf dem Grunde, hat aus der Geschlechtlichkeit etwas Unreines gemacht
quote.translation: Only Christianity, with its ressentiment against life at bottom, made sexuality something impure.

image.credit: Friedrich Hermann Hartmann · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: In The Birth of Tragedy Nietzsche explains Greek tragedy as a union of two drives. The Apollonian is the drive to form, measure and beautiful illusion, like a dream; the Dionysian is ecstatic, boundary-dissolving intoxication. Tragedy lets us glimpse the terrible truth of existence and still affirm it.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 7206

quote.text: dass die Fortentwickelung der Kunst an die Duplicität des Apollinischen und des Dionysischen gebunden ist
quote.translation: that the continuing development of art is bound up with the duality of the Apollonian and the Dionysian.

image.credit: Friedrich Hermann Hartmann · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Nietzsche's diagnosis of modern Europe: belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, and with it the foundation of Western values has collapsed, even if people have not yet noticed. The danger is nihilism; the task is a revaluation of all values.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 7205

quote.text: Gott ist todt; an seinem Mitleiden mit den Menschen ist Gott gestorben.
quote.translation: God is dead; God has died of his pity for man.

image.credit: Friedrich Hermann Hartmann · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Heidegger's word for the kind of being that we ourselves are: the being for whom its own being is an issue. He avoids 'consciousness' or 'subject' because Dasein is always already in a world, among things and others. In ordinary German it just means 'existence'.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against the Niemeyer edition of Sein und Zeit (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/sein_und_zeit, fuzzy-matched)

quote.text: Das Dasein ist ein Seiendes, das nicht nur unter anderem Seienden vorkommt. Es ist vielmehr dadurch ontisch ausgezeichnet, daß es diesem Seienden in seinem Sein um dieses Sein selbst geht.
quote.translation: Dasein is an entity that does not just occur among other entities. Rather, it is ontically distinguished by the fact that, in its very being, that being is an issue for it.

image.credit: Willy Pragher · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Dasein is not a mind looking out at a world of objects; it is from the start absorbed in a world of tasks and tools. The hyphens mark a single unified phenomenon. A hammer is first encountered in use, ready-to-hand, not as a thing with properties.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against the Niemeyer edition of Sein und Zeit (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/sein_und_zeit, fuzzy-matched)

quote.text: Der zusammengesetzte Ausdruck »In-der-Welt-sein« zeigt schon in seiner Prägung an, daß mit ihm ein einheitliches Phänomen gemeint ist.
quote.translation: The compound expression 'being-in-the-world' shows in its very coinage that it stands for a unitary phenomenon.

image.credit: Willy Pragher · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Death is Dasein's ownmost possibility: no one can die my death for me. By facing it in anxiety rather than fleeing into 'they say everyone dies', Dasein can live authentically, owning its finite life.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against the Niemeyer edition of Sein und Zeit (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/sein_und_zeit, fuzzy-matched)

quote.text: Der Tod ist eine Weise zu sein, die das Dasein übernimmt, sobald es ist.
quote.translation: Death is a way to be, which Dasein takes over as soon as it is.

image.credit: Willy Pragher · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Late Wittgenstein compares using words to playing games: there is no single essence of language, only many activities bound up with forms of life, such as giving orders, telling jokes, praying. The meaning of a word is its use in the language.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Wittgenstein Project (German text of the 1953 edition)

quote.text: Ich werde auch das Ganze: der Sprache und der Tätigkeiten, mit denen sie verwoben ist, das »Sprachspiel« nennen.
quote.translation: I shall also call the whole, consisting of language and the activities into which it is woven, the 'language-game'.

image.credit: Moritz Nähr · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: What do all games have in common? Nothing, says Wittgenstein: only overlapping similarities, like the resemblances among members of a family. Many concepts work this way, so asking for a strict definition can be a mistake.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Wittgenstein Project (German text of the 1953 edition)

quote.text: Ich kann diese Ähnlichkeiten nicht besser charakterisieren als durch das Wort »Familienähnlichkeiten«
quote.translation: I can think of no better expression to characterise these similarities than 'family resemblances'.

image.credit: Moritz Nähr · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons
